items.lessonTitle: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset

neighbors.heading: a lamp at dusk
neighbors.text: Today a match was struck at dusk, and the week went quiet. Many Hindu homes light a small lamp at dusk too, a diya by the family shrine, as day turns to evening. Families often say a short Sanskrit verse that greets the lamp's light as bringing what is good and auspicious, and children fold their hands to the flame.
neighbors.difference: Shabbat candles open a weekly day of rest, lit before sunset so no fire is kindled after. The Hindu evening lamp is often lit every day, and the flame itself is honored, often waved before God in aarti.
neighbors.shared: a small flame can tell a whole house the day has turned.
neighbors.sources: evening lamp verse, "Shubham karoti kalyanam" (paraphrase) · lighting the lamp at sandhya, dusk (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a day of gathering
neighbors.text: Today two flames opened a holy day. Muslims keep a holy day each week too: Friday, Jumu'ah, the day of gathering. The Qur'an says: "O ye who believe! When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading." The shop pauses, and people pray side by side.
neighbors.difference: Shabbat is a full day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Jumu'ah centers on a midday prayer together; the next verse says that when the prayer is ended, people may go out again and seek God's bounty.
neighbors.shared: the week has a holy pause, and you're invited into it.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 62:9 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 62:10 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the first commandment
neighbors.text: Today six words were said under a covering hand. Christians know them too, because Jesus said them. Asked which commandment comes first, he answered with the Shema: "The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord." Then he went on: love God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength.
neighbors.difference: Jews say the Shema as Israel's own witness to one God. Christians also confess one God, and the historic creeds understand that one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, which Jewish teaching does not.
neighbors.shared: your first words can be a reminder of what matters most.
neighbors.sources: Mark 12:29-30 (KJV) · Deuteronomy 6:4

neighbors.heading: one, first
neighbors.text: Today you heard six words that end with one. Sikh scripture begins the same way. The very first word of the Guru Granth Sahib is Ik Onkar: one creator, the one that is everything. The opening lines, the Mool Mantar, go on to call this one true by name, the creator, without fear, without hate. Many Sikhs say it at dawn.
neighbors.difference: The Shema is a command to listen, said to the people of Israel about the God of the Torah. Ik Onkar opens Guru Nanak's teaching of one formless creator, known through the Guru's word and remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: both begin with one, said out loud.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (paraphrase) · Deuteronomy 6:4

neighbors.heading: grace before meals
neighbors.text: Today a two-second blessing came before the bite. Catholics pause at the table too, often with the sign of the cross and a short grace children learn early: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." The food is named as a gift before anyone eats.
neighbors.difference: A bracha blesses God, the source, and has different endings for different kinds of food. Catholic grace asks God to bless the people and the gifts, and is prayed through Christ.
neighbors.shared: the food on your plate came from somewhere, and you can say so.
neighbors.sources: traditional Catholic grace before meals

neighbors.heading: eat on purpose
neighbors.text: Today a small pause came between wanting and having. Buddhist monks keep a pause like that. In one of the Buddha's teachings, a monk reflects before eating: this food isn't for fun or for show, but to keep this body going, to ease hunger, and to support the practice. Many Buddhists still say a short meal reflection before they eat.
neighbors.difference: The Jewish blessing thanks God as the source of the food. The Buddhist reflection isn't addressed to a creator; it trains attention, so eating stays honest and simple.
neighbors.shared: a pause before eating turns a snack into a moment.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta, reflection on almsfood (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: love and mercy between you
neighbors.text: Today the Torah's first "not good" was being alone. The Qur'an counts companionship among God's signs: "He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." This verse is often read at Muslim weddings, a reminder that a partner is meant to be rest, not just help.
neighbors.difference: Genesis tells it as a story: the second person is made from the first one's side. The Qur'an speaks of mates created from yourselves without telling that story, and names the bond itself, love and mercy, as a sign of God.
neighbors.shared: people were made to find rest in each other.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 30:21 (Pickthall 1930) · Genesis 2:18 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: unnoticed
neighbors.text: Today God looked at someone alone and said it's not good. A psychologist said it his way. William James wrote: "No more fiendish punishment could be devised, were such a thing physically possible, than that one should be turned loose in society and remain absolutely unnoticed by all the members thereof." Each of us, he said, has a social self: the recognition we get from others.
neighbors.difference: The Torah hears it from God at the start of the world, and answers with a partner who faces you. James arrives at it by watching people, without any claim about who made them.
neighbors.shared: nobody is meant to go unseen.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology, chapter 10 (William James 1890) · Genesis 2:18 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: one human family
neighbors.text: Today Cain asked if he was his brother's keeper, and the Torah kept answering yes. Sikhs answer with a whole kitchen. At the gurdwara, the langar serves a free meal to anyone, side by side on the floor, whoever they are. A line attributed to Guru Gobind Singh says to recognize the whole human race as one.
neighbors.difference: The Torah answers Cain with commandments: don't stand by your neighbor's blood, love your neighbor. Sikhs root the answer in seva, selfless service, and in seeing the one creator's light in everyone.
neighbors.shared: the person next to you is yours to look after.
neighbors.sources: Akal Ustat, Dasam Granth, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh (paraphrase) · langar, the gurdwara kitchen (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the world is one family
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said yes, you are your brother's keeper. Hindus have a famous phrase for that circle drawn wide: vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the world is one family. An Upanishad says that thinking "this one is mine, that one is a stranger" is how small minds count; for the generous-hearted, the whole earth is family.
neighbors.difference: The Torah answers through a story, a crime and a law, and God's own care for Cain. The Upanishad speaks as wisdom about the wide heart, without commandments and without a single story behind it.
neighbors.shared: nobody is a stranger to a big enough heart.
neighbors.sources: Maha Upanishad 6.71-72 (paraphrase) · Leviticus 19:16, 18 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: the going forth
neighbors.text: Today Abram left country, birthplace and father's house. The Buddha's story has a leaving too. In his own telling, he was young, with black hair, and his parents wept; still he shaved his head, put on a simple robe, and went forth from home into homelessness, to look for what doesn't decay. Buddhists still call becoming a monk "going forth."
neighbors.difference: Abram goes because God calls him, toward a land God will show him. In this sutta, the Buddha goes by his own search, looking for an end to suffering.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the road starts before you know where it goes.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 26, Ariyapariyesana Sutta (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not knowing whither
neighbors.text: Today Abram went before he knew. Christians hold him up for exactly that. The letter to the Hebrews says: "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went." And the first disciples, called at the shore, "straightway left their nets, and followed him."
neighbors.difference: For Jews, Abraham is the father of the covenant with Israel, and the call leads to the land. Christians read him as a model of faith fulfilled in Jesus, and Jesus' call is to follow him.
neighbors.shared: trust can mean taking the first step without a map.
neighbors.sources: Hebrews 11:8 (KJV) · Matthew 4:20 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: made for each other
neighbors.text: Today an old man ran in the heat to welcome strangers. A Roman emperor wrote a note to himself that runs the same way. Marcus Aurelius, in his private journal: "Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them." For him, every person, stranger or not, was kin by nature, made to work together.
neighbors.difference: Abraham's welcome is lived before God, and the tradition says his guests were angels. Marcus grounds it in shared human nature and reason: we're made to work together, like hands and feet.
neighbors.shared: the stranger in front of you is someone to make room for.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 8.59 (Long 1862) · Meditations 2.1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: received like Christ
neighbors.text: Today Abraham ran to three tired strangers. Catholics hear Jesus in the same scene: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Whoever welcomes the least, he said, welcomes him. Monasteries built rules on it. Saint Benedict told his monks to receive every guest who arrives as Christ himself, with a bow and water for their hands and feet.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis the guests turn out to be messengers of God, and welcoming them is a commandment kept for its own sake. Catholics see Christ himself in the guest, so the welcome is given to him.
neighbors.shared: a guest at your door can be a holy moment.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:35, 40 (Douay-Rheims) · Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 53 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: food for every creature
neighbors.text: Today Rebekah watered a stranger's camels without being asked. Many Hindu households set aside a little for animals too. Old Vedic teaching names five daily offerings, and one is for all beings: food for birds, dogs, cows and anyone hungry. Some families still put out the first roti for a cow, or grain for birds, before they eat.
neighbors.difference: Chesed is kindness past what's owed, praised as the way of God and the world's foundation. The Hindu offering is a daily duty, one of five daily offerings: to gods, ancestors, sages, people and all living things.
neighbors.shared: kindness notices the thirsty one nobody asked about.
neighbors.sources: Shatapatha Brahmana 11.5.6.1, the five great offerings (paraphrase) · bhuta yajna, offering to all beings (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: water for a thirsty dog
neighbors.text: Today the test was who notices the camels. Muslims tell a story the Prophet told. A man walking in the heat found a well, climbed down and drank. Coming up, he saw a dog panting, licking the mud from thirst. He climbed down again, filled his shoe with water, and held it up for the dog. God thanked him, and forgave him.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, Rebekah's kindness shows she's the one to carry Abraham's family forward. In the hadith, a nameless man's kindness to an animal is itself the whole story, and wins God's forgiveness.
neighbors.shared: kindness to an animal counts.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2363 and Sahih Muslim 2244, the man and the thirsty dog (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: he ran
neighbors.text: Today Esau ran and fell on his brother's neck. Jesus told a parable that uses the same picture. A son who wasted everything comes home, rehearsing an apology. "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The one who was wronged closes the distance.
neighbors.difference: Genesis tells a family repair that stays honest and partial: they weep, then go separate ways. Christians read Jesus' parable as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who comes back.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the one who was hurt runs first.
neighbors.sources: Luke 15:20 (KJV) · Genesis 33:4 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: where there is forgiveness
neighbors.text: Today two brothers who'd been enemies wept on each other's necks. Sikh scripture has a short line about that moment. In a verse of Kabir kept in the Guru Granth Sahib: where there is greed, there is death; where there is forgiveness, there God is. Sikh teaching counts forgiveness, khima, among the qualities a Sikh is asked to grow.
neighbors.difference: The Torah shows forgiveness in a story without naming it, and the rabbis even argue whether Esau's kiss was sincere. The Sikh verse names forgiveness directly as the place where God is present.
neighbors.shared: making peace can start with one person running.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Kabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: Rachel bewailing
neighbors.text: Today Rachel was buried by the road, and she still weeps for her children. Catholics hear her voice at Christmas. Matthew's Gospel quotes Jeremiah when Herod's soldiers kill the baby boys of Bethlehem: "Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." The Church remembers those children every December 28 as the Holy Innocents.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish memory Rachel weeps for her people in exile, and God promises they'll come back. Matthew hears her crying over the infants killed when Jesus was born, and reads the verse as fulfilled there.
neighbors.shared: a mother's grief is never too small for heaven to hear.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 2:18 (Douay-Rheims) · Jeremiah 31:14 (JPS 1917; 31:15 in English Bibles) · feast of the Holy Innocents (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mustard seed
neighbors.text: Today a mother wept for her children. Buddhists tell of Kisa Gotami, whose little boy died. She carried him door to door, begging for medicine. The Buddha asked her for a mustard seed from a house where no one had died. Every door had a loss. She came back with no seed, and not alone anymore.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah answers Rachel with a promise: your children will come home. The Buddha gives Kisa Gotami no promise of return; he helps her see that loss touches every house, and teaches a path through it.
neighbors.shared: grief, everywhere it lands, deserves company.
neighbors.sources: story of Kisa Gotami, Dhammapada commentary and Therigatha commentary (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no blame today
neighbors.text: Today Joseph told his brothers who he was. The Qur'an tells Joseph's story too, in a whole surah named for him, Yusuf. When his brothers finally stand before him, he says: "Have no fear this day! May Allah forgive you." Later, with his family around him, he says God was kind to him, since He took him out of the prison.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, Joseph says "it was not you that sent me hither, but God," and readers argue over what he means. In the Qur'an, Joseph is a prophet, and the story is called the best of stories, told as a lesson in patience and trust.
neighbors.shared: a hard road can still lead somewhere good.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 12:92 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 12:100 (paraphrase) · Qur'an 12:3 (paraphrase) · Genesis 45:8 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: understood backwards
neighbors.text: Today Joseph looked back over the pit and the prison and saw a road. A philosopher wrote about that kind of looking. Søren Kierkegaard noted in his journal that life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards. You make meaning looking back; you still have to walk on, not knowing.
neighbors.difference: Joseph names God as the one who sent him ahead. Kierkegaard was deeply Christian, but this line stands on its own: many people use it with no claim about who, if anyone, was steering.
neighbors.shared: looking back, you might find a path you couldn't see.
neighbors.sources: Søren Kierkegaard, Journals, 1843 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: fear no one
neighbors.text: Today two midwives feared God more than a king, and quietly said no. Sikhs have a line for that kind of courage. Guru Tegh Bahadur wrote that the wise person frightens no one, and is afraid of no one. Sikhs remember him for standing up for other people's freedom of faith, even when an emperor demanded otherwise.
neighbors.difference: Shiphrah and Puah never say a word against Pharaoh; they outwit him and walk away. Sikh memory honors open witness, and Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his life rather than give in.
neighbors.shared: some orders you can quietly refuse.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9 (paraphrase) · Exodus 1:17 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: the boy who wouldn't bow
neighbors.text: Today the first people to defy Pharaoh were two working women. Hindus tell of a child who defied a king. Prahlad's father, the demon king Hiranyakashipu, ordered everyone to worship him alone. Prahlad kept praying to Vishnu. Threats didn't move him. In the end Vishnu came as Narasimha, half man, half lion, to protect him.
neighbors.difference: In Exodus no miracle saves the midwives; their own wit does, and God makes them houses. In the Hindu story, God appears in a fierce form to rescue Prahlad from his father.
neighbors.shared: courage can come from people the powerful overlook.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana, book 7, Prahlad and Narasimha (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hatred stops with love
neighbors.text: Today the angels were told not to sing over the drowning. Buddhists have an old verse about enemies too. The Dhammapada says: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." It's among the first verses in the book, and many Buddhists learn it young.
neighbors.difference: The Talmud lets the people who were saved sing, and only asks that nobody celebrate suffering. The Buddhist verse goes after hatred itself: only its opposite ever ends it.
neighbors.shared: even an enemy's pain isn't something to cheer.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 5 (Max Müller 1881) · Talmud, Megillah 10b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: love your enemies
neighbors.text: Today God hushed the angels, because the Egyptians were drowning. Christians hear a teaching of Jesus there. In the Sermon on the Mount he says: "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." Christians share Proverbs too: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth."
neighbors.difference: The rabbis let the rescued sing and forbid gloating; the Torah also asks you to help an enemy's fallen donkey. Christians hear Jesus' call to love and pray for enemies, and see it lived in his death.
neighbors.shared: people who hurt us are still somebody's children.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:44 (KJV) · Proverbs 24:17 (KJV) · Exodus 23:5 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rich in letting go
neighbors.text: Today manna fell, enough for one day, and hoarding it went bad. Henry David Thoreau went to live in a small cabin by a pond to test how little he needed. He wrote: "a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone." And, more simply: "Simplify, simplify."
neighbors.difference: Manna is a gift from God, a daily school of trust. Thoreau's "enough" is a choice he made himself, an experiment in living, with no promise that anything would fall from the sky.
neighbors.shared: enough for today can be enough.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, chapter 2 (Thoreau 1854)

neighbors.heading: daily bread
neighbors.text: Today the manna came one day at a time. Catholics pray for bread the same way: "Give us this day our daily bread." And Jesus pointed back to the manna. In John's Gospel he says: "Your fathers did eat manna in the desert, and are dead," and calls himself the living bread which came down from heaven.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, manna is God's care in the wilderness, remembered every Shabbat in two loaves. Catholics also read it as a sign pointing ahead to the Eucharist, which they believe is Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: you can ask for just today, and trust there's enough.
neighbors.sources: Luke 11:3 (Douay-Rheims) · John 6:49-51 (Douay-Rheims)

items.lessonTitle: A guest at the Friday table

neighbors.heading: the guest is God
neighbors.text: Today you were a guest at a Friday table, and nobody expected you to know the words. Hindus have a short line for the host's side. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students home with advice: honor your mother, your father, your teacher, and atithi devo bhava, treat the guest as God.
neighbors.difference: The rabbis rank welcoming guests above receiving the Divine Presence, but the guest is still a guest. The Upanishad asks you to honor the guest as God; Jewish teaching sees God's image in a guest, never the guest as God.
neighbors.shared: a stranger at your table is someone to honor.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (paraphrase) · Talmud, Shabbat 127a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: honor your guest
neighbors.text: Today the Friday table made room for someone who didn't know the words. Muslims treat welcoming guests as part of faith itself. The Prophet said: whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let them honor their guest. Many Muslim homes take pride in feeding visitors first and best, and urging one more helping.
neighbors.difference: A Shabbat table has its own blessings, wine and loaves, and the guest is welcomed into them. Muslim hospitality has no set weekly meal; the duty to honor a guest goes with every visit, any day.
neighbors.shared: a full table is better with one more chair.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018 and Sahih Muslim 47, honoring the guest (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: safely to this morning
neighbors.text: Today the first words of the day were thank you. Christians have morning prayers that start the same way. An old Anglican prayer book prays each morning: "O Lord, our heavenly Father, Almighty and everlasting God, who hast safely brought us to the beginning of this day." Thanks first, then the ask: keep us through it.
neighbors.difference: Modeh Ani thanks God for returning the soul, and uses no name of God, so it can be said before washing your hands. The Christian collect names God as Father and is prayed through Jesus Christ.
neighbors.shared: waking up is a gift worth noticing.
neighbors.sources: Book of Common Prayer 1662, Morning Prayer, Third Collect, for Grace

neighbors.heading: the ambrosial hour
neighbors.text: Today you thanked God before your feet touched the floor. Sikhs treasure the first hours too. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says: in the ambrosial hours before dawn, chant the true Name and reflect on God's greatness. Many Sikhs rise early, bathe, and recite the Japji as the day begins.
neighbors.difference: Modeh Ani is one short line of thanks for getting your soul back. The Sikh morning is a longer discipline: rising before dawn and remembering the Name, which Sikhs call naam simran.
neighbors.shared: the first minutes of the day can belong to thanks.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, pauri 4 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: eternal rest
neighbors.text: Today you learned three words for the worst news. Catholics have a short prayer for that moment too, said at gravesides and in prayers for the dead: "Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them." The Church also prays for the dead at Mass, so the grieving never pray alone.
neighbors.difference: Baruch Dayan HaEmet blesses God and explains nothing. The Catholic prayer is said for the person who died, and rests on the Church's hope of resurrection in Christ.
neighbors.shared: even in grief, there are words to hold onto.
neighbors.sources: traditional Catholic prayer for the dead, "Eternal rest" · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1032 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all things pass
neighbors.text: Today the first word after a death was a blessing. At many Buddhist funerals, monks chant a verse the scriptures place at the Buddha's own death: impermanent are all conditioned things; they rise and pass away; their stilling is peace. It explains nothing about why. It says what is true, and lets everyone sit with it.
neighbors.difference: The Jewish blessing speaks to God, the true judge, in the middle of loss. The Buddhist verse speaks of impermanence and peace, without addressing a creator.
neighbors.shared: some moments need a few true words, then quiet.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the verse "anicca vata sankhara" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: forgive and overlook
neighbors.text: Today you met a prayer that forgives everyone before sleep. The Qur'an asks for that kind of heart: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" Many Muslims also have their own bedtime words: short surahs recited before sleep, and a line lying down: in Your name, O God, I die and I live.
neighbors.difference: The bedtime Shema is a nightly declaration, forgiving anyone by name or not. In the Qur'an the call to forgive comes as guidance for all times, and the bedtime prayers come from the Prophet's own practice.
neighbors.shared: it's easier to sleep with nothing held against anyone.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 24:22 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari 6312, bedtime supplication (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the evening review
neighbors.text: Today the day ended with I forgive you. A Roman philosopher ended his days with a review. Seneca wrote that each night, when the lamp was out, he went over his whole day, hiding nothing from himself. Where he'd slipped, he told himself: see that you don't do that again; this time I forgive you. Then he slept well.
neighbors.difference: The bedtime Shema forgives others and turns to God before sleep. Seneca's review is a conversation with yourself, an honest look at your own day, and the forgiveness he gives is mostly his own.
neighbors.shared: putting the day down gently helps you rest.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, On Anger 3.36 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the day of release
neighbors.text: Today eight lights went in the window, to be seen. Sikhs light up their own story in the darker part of the year. On Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release, they remember Guru Hargobind leaving prison and, tradition says, bringing fifty-two other prisoners out with him. The Golden Temple in Amritsar glows with lamps.
neighbors.difference: Hanukkah remembers a rededicated Temple and a jar of oil that lasted, lit night after night. Bandi Chhor Divas remembers a Guru's release, kept on one night, alongside Diwali.
neighbors.shared: light in the window says freedom is worth remembering.
neighbors.sources: Bandi Chhor Divas, Guru Hargobind's release (paraphrase, tradition)

neighbors.heading: rows of lamps
neighbors.text: Today a small light went in the window for the street to see. Hindus fill whole streets with them. At Diwali, the festival of lights, families set rows of clay lamps on doorsteps and windowsills. Many tell it as the night Rama came home to Ayodhya, and the people lit the way.
neighbors.difference: Hanukkah remembers a historical revolt and a rededicated Temple, with lights added one a night. Diwali carries different stories in different regions, Rama's return among them, and honors Lakshmi in many homes.
neighbors.shared: a light in the dark is meant to be seen.
neighbors.sources: Diwali and Rama's return to Ayodhya (paraphrase, tradition)

items.lessonTitle: Passover: a seat at the seder

neighbors.heading: never eat without sharing
neighbors.text: Today the seder opened with: let all who are hungry come and eat. The Buddha said something close. If people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, he said, they would not eat without giving, even if it were their last bite. Many Buddhists still offer food each morning to monks who walk past with bowls.
neighbors.difference: The seder invitation is said aloud at a family meal, remembering a people's own hunger as slaves. The Buddha's teaching is about generosity as a practice that frees the giver, without one founding story behind it.
neighbors.shared: there's room for one more at the table.
neighbors.sources: Itivuttaka 26 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: call the poor
neighbors.text: Today the door opened with an invitation to anyone hungry. Jesus told his host to set a table like that: "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind." They can't repay you, he said, and that's the point. Christians still serve community meals built on the same idea.
neighbors.difference: The seder welcomes the hungry into a night of Jewish memory, the Exodus told again. Christians connect their table to Jesus' last supper, which the Gospels set at Passover time, and to his welcome of outsiders.
neighbors.shared: a feast is best with the people who can't pay you back.
neighbors.sources: Luke 14:13-14 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: can they suffer?
neighbors.text: Today Jewish law said: no needless pain for animals, and feed them before you eat. A philosopher reached the same place by asking one question. Jeremy Bentham wrote of animals: "The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?" If they can, he said, their pain counts.
neighbors.difference: Jewish law protects animals because God's tender mercies are over all creation, worked out in specific commandments. Bentham's reason is the suffering itself, weighed by human reason, without a command from above.
neighbors.shared: animals feel, and that's reason enough to be gentle.
neighbors.sources: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), chapter 17, note

neighbors.heading: every creature
neighbors.text: Today Jewish law asked for kindness to animals, even your enemy's donkey. Catholics teach it too. The Catechism says animals are God's creatures, that people owe them kindness, and that causing them to suffer or die needlessly goes against human dignity. Saint Francis of Assisi preached to birds, and on his feast day many churches bless pets.
neighbors.difference: Jewish law spells out exact rules, like the mother bird and the ox's muzzle. Catholic teaching names the principle and leaves most details to conscience, while allowing animals to be used for food and work.
neighbors.shared: every creature is worth a little tenderness.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2416-2418 (paraphrase) · Saint Francis, blessing of animals (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: study and teaching
neighbors.text: Today learning was called equal to every kindness. An Upanishad says something close. In the Taittiriya, a teacher lists the good things in a life, truth, self-control, calm, guests, children, and after each one adds the same words: and study and teaching. Whatever you're doing, keep learning and keep passing it on.
neighbors.difference: Talmud Torah is study of one revealed teaching, the Torah, as a commandment. Hindu svadhyaya can mean studying the Veda and other sacred texts, and also study of the self.
neighbors.shared: learning can be a kind of prayer.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.9 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the first word was read
neighbors.text: Today study was called worship. The Qur'an's first revealed word, Muslims say, was a command to read: "Read: In the name of thy Lord who createth." And the Qur'an gives a short prayer for anyone learning: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Muslims have long gathered in mosques and circles to study together.
neighbors.difference: In Judaism, study centers on the Torah and the rabbis' arguments over it. Muslims study the Qur'an as God's own word and the Prophet's example, with the scholars' rulings built on both.
neighbors.shared: every honest question can be a way toward God.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 96:1 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 20:114 (Pickthall 1930)

neighbors.heading: he stood up to read
neighbors.text: Today the Torah was read aloud, with the room listening. The Gospels show Jesus reading aloud in a synagogue. In Nazareth, "as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read. And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias." Churches still read scripture aloud on Sundays.
neighbors.difference: Jews read the Torah from a handwritten scroll, in Hebrew, usually in a yearly cycle. Christians read from both Testaments, mostly in their own languages, and hear the Gospel as the high point.
neighbors.shared: holy words land differently when you hear them together.
neighbors.sources: Luke 4:16-17 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: the living Guru
neighbors.text: Today a scroll was carried, read with a pointer and treated with care. Sikhs honor their scripture with great care too. The Guru Granth Sahib rests under a canopy, is waved over with a whisk, and is put to rest at night. Each morning it's opened at random, and the first verse read is the day's word.
neighbors.difference: The Torah scroll is God's teaching, handled with great honor, but never called a person. Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as their living Guru, the last and lasting teacher.
neighbors.shared: words can be honored like a guest in the house.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, prakash and hukamnama (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Bereshit: you can rule over it (Genesis 4:7)

neighbors.heading: overcome evil with good
neighbors.text: Today the urge crouched at the door, and God said you can rule it. Catholics teach that the pull toward wrong stays in us; they call it concupiscence, and say it can be fought with grace. Saint Paul put it plainly: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good."
neighbors.difference: The rabbis say the urge was made by God and isn't simply bad, since it also drives building and family. Catholics trace the pull to the fall of the first humans, and see grace through Christ as the help to win.
neighbors.shared: you're stronger than the thing that pulls at you.
neighbors.sources: Romans 12:21 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 405, 1264 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the greatest conqueror
neighbors.text: Today a voice told Cain he could master what crouched at the door. The Dhammapada says the same about strength: "If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors." Pirkei Avot says almost the same. Who is mighty? The one who rules their own urge.
neighbors.difference: In the Torah, the urge is part of how God made people, ruled with the help of Torah. Buddhists see craving as a root of suffering, tamed by mindfulness and the path, without a creator involved.
neighbors.shared: the hardest win is over your own worst moment.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 103 (Max Müller 1881) · Pirkei Avot 4:1 (paraphrase)
